::: {.lead}
*Pixel Harbor* is a small mobile-game studio. It wants to hire a junior game
tester. The tester will not write code, but will use a computer all day:
signing in safely, recording bugs, writing reports, sorting results in a
spreadsheet. The studio asks every candidate: *"Describe your digital
skills."* Most students answer: "I am good with computers." That is not
enough. In this lab session you learn what digital skills are, how a European
framework describes them clearly, and why employers need them. You also make
your own digital skills profile on the lab computer.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary digital-skills digital-literacy digital-competence digcomp competence-area proficiency-level labour-market lifelong-learning >}}

## 1.1 Digital skills, digital literacy and digital competence

This course uses three words, from the smallest idea to the biggest
(@fig-circles).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — Skills, literacy and competence"}
**Digital skills** are the practical abilities to use digital devices, apps
and networks: for example, formatting a document or sharing a folder.
**Digital literacy** adds understanding: finding, checking and sharing
information in a careful and safe way. **Digital competence** is the
biggest: using digital technology with confidence and responsibility for
study, work and life. It combines *knowledge*, *skills* and *attitudes*.
:::

![Skills, literacy and competence: each one contains the one before.](images/skills-circles.png){#fig-circles width=66%}

The difference matters. A student who types fast and knows every menu of a
word processor has good skills. A student who can also check if a website is
reliable, protect their account, respect the licence of an image and choose
the right tool for a task is digitally competent.

We often describe digital skills at three levels (@tbl-levels).

| Level | What the person does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| basic | uses devices and common apps for everyday tasks | sends e-mail, searches the web, fills in an online form |
| intermediate | uses special apps well at work | makes a chart in a spreadsheet, edits a short video |
| advanced | creates and manages digital technology | programs a game, runs servers, protects networks |

: Three levels of digital skills. {#tbl-levels}

Most jobs need the basic and intermediate levels in many tools, not the
advanced level in one tool. This course teaches exactly this.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — One day of a game tester"}
A junior game tester at a mobile-game studio spends one day like this:

1. signs in to the studio's systems with a password and a code on the phone;
2. installs the newest version of the game on three Android phones and an
   iPhone;
3. plays it, records a short video of a bug and cuts it;
4. writes a clear bug report with steps, the video and the phone model in a
   shared tracker;
5. sorts the day's bugs in a spreadsheet by how serious they are.

None of these tasks is programming, but each one is a digital skill. A tester
without one of them slows down the whole team.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Your digital week"}
1. Write five things that you did on a computer or a phone this week (for
   example "sent a voice message", "edited a photo", "filled in a form").
2. Next to each one, write its level: basic, intermediate or advanced.

*Your result:* the list of five tasks with their levels. Most of them are
probably basic: this course moves them to intermediate.
:::

## 1.2 The DigComp framework

To teach and test digital competence in the same way everywhere, the European
Commission publishes the **Digital Competence Framework for Citizens**, called
**DigComp**. The current version, DigComp 2.2 (2022), has **five competence
areas** with **21 competences** in total (@fig-digcomp).

![The five competence areas of DigComp 2.2 and their 21 competences.](images/digcomp-areas.png){#fig-digcomp width=96%}

| Area | In simple words | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Information and data literacy | find, check and keep information | checking if a website is reliable |
| 2 Communication and collaboration | talk, share and work together online | writing polite messages in a team chat |
| 3 Digital content creation | make documents, pictures and videos | editing a short video |
| 4 Safety | protect devices, data and health | using a screen lock |
| 5 Problem solving | solve technical problems, learn new tools | finding out how to fix a printer |

: The five areas of DigComp 2.2. {#tbl-digcomp}

For each competence, DigComp describes **proficiency levels**: how well a
person can do it. There are eight levels in four groups (@fig-levels-ds).

![The DigComp proficiency levels in four groups.](images/proficiency.png){#fig-levels-ds width=84%}

| Group | Levels | A person at this level … |
|---|---|---|
| foundation | 1–2 | does simple tasks, with help |
| intermediate | 3–4 | does normal tasks alone |
| advanced | 5–6 | does different tasks and helps others |
| highly specialised | 7–8 | solves hard problems and leads others |

: DigComp proficiency groups. {#tbl-bands}

DigComp is used in real life. Employers use its words in job advertisements.
Universities use it to plan courses. The European CV (Europass) asks people to
describe their digital skills with its areas and levels. Self-check tools ask
questions for each area and show a profile, so that a learner knows where to
start.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — Tasks of a game studio in DigComp"}
Four tasks of a game studio, with their DigComp area:

1. Checking if a forum post about a new phone is reliable before using its
   numbers: **information and data literacy** (area 1).
2. Writing polite, clear messages in the team chat: **communication and
   collaboration** (area 2).
3. Checking the licence of a free sound effect before using it in a trailer:
   **digital content creation** (area 3).
4. Noticing that you cannot make a chart yet, and taking an online course:
   **problem solving** (area 5).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Digital competence means programming." No: programming is only *one* of the
21 competences. A person can be very competent in information,
communication, safety and problem solving without writing code.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Your DigComp profile"}
Open the **DigComp self-check** below (or scan its QR code) on the lab
computer.

1. For each competence, choose the level that describes you honestly. Your
   answers stay in this browser only.
2. Look at your profile. Find your strongest area and your weakest area.
3. Save or print your profile as a PDF. You will put it in your course
   folder in the next lab session.

*Your result:* your profile, and one learning goal for your weakest area.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/digcomp-check.html" poster="sims/digcomp-check.png" title="DigComp self-check" height="760" >}}

## 1.3 Digital skills and the labour market

The **labour market** is where workers offer their skills and employers look
for the skills they need. Three changes have put digital skills in the centre
of it.

1. **Work is digital.** In almost every job (shops, hospitals, media,
   transport) people now use digital tools. Job advertisements without any
   digital skills have become rare.
2. **Automation.** Software and artificial intelligence now do many routine
   tasks. So employers need people who can use, check and combine these
   tools. Jobs change more often than they disappear.
3. **Government targets.** Governments see digital skills as important as
   roads. The European Union, for example, wants at least 80 % of adults to
   have at least basic digital skills by 2030.

Tools change quickly, so no diploma can teach every app that a graduate will
use. Employers therefore value two things more than one program: the ability
to learn a new tool alone, and the habit of learning during the whole working
life, called **lifelong learning**.

### Digital skills in the games industry

The games industry is completely digital, its tools change every year, and
its teams often work in different countries. Every role in a studio, not only
programming, needs its own mix of digital skills (@fig-studio, @tbl-roles).

![Every role in a game studio depends on digital tools.](images/studio.png){#fig-studio width=92%}

| Role | Main digital tasks | DigComp areas |
|---|---|---|
| game tester | bug reports, screen videos, spreadsheets of results | 2, 3, 1 |
| game designer | design documents, presentations, data about players | 3, 1 |
| producer | plans in the cloud, shared documents, budgets | 2, 1 |
| community and marketing | social media, web pages, numbers about players | 2, 3, 1 |
| everyone | safe accounts, privacy, licences, good manners online | 4, 3, 2 |

: Digital skills in game-industry roles. {#tbl-roles}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.3 — Reading a job advertisement"}
A studio looks for a "Junior Community Manager". The advertisement says:
*"manage our social channels; prepare weekly reports in spreadsheets; create
simple graphics and short videos; handle player data responsibly."*

1. Managing channels and talking to players: area 2 (communication and
   collaboration).
2. Weekly reports in spreadsheets: area 1 (information and data).
3. Graphics and videos: area 3 (content creation).
4. Handling player data responsibly: area 4 (safety: personal data and
   privacy).
5. A candidate can compare this list with their own DigComp profile to find
   their gaps (area 5) before applying.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · A real job advertisement"}
1. On a job website, find one real advertisement for a job in games, design,
   media or marketing.
2. Copy four requirements from it into a document.
3. Next to each requirement, write its DigComp area.
4. Compare with your DigComp profile: which requirement is your biggest gap?

*Your result:* a short document with four requirements, their areas, and your
biggest gap. Save it as `job-advert_digcomp.docx`.
:::

## Case study: Pixel Harbor Studio

*Pixel Harbor* is a made-up mobile-game studio with eight employees, who work
partly from home. It is hiring two juniors, a game tester and a marketing
assistant. It asks every candidate to describe their digital skills with the
DigComp areas and levels. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
this studio.

## Further reading

Evans, Martin and Poatsy, *Technology in Action*, 18th ed., Chapter 1 ("The
Impact of Technology in a Changing World"); European Commission, Joint
Research Centre, *DigComp 2.2: The Digital Competence Framework for Citizens*,
2022.

## Exercises

1. What is the difference between digital skills and digital competence? Give
   an example of a person who has the first but not the second.
2. Name the five DigComp areas.
3. Which DigComp area is each task in? (a) installing the security updates of
   a phone; (b) organising sources in folders; (c) writing a simple script; (d) choosing a video tool for a new task.
4. A student can share a file when a friend explains each step, but not
   alone. Which proficiency group is this?
5. Why does automation make digital skills more important, not less?
6. Choose one role in @tbl-roles. Write two digital tasks it needs, each with
   its DigComp area.
7. *Pixel Harbor*: write three lines about your own digital skills for the
   tester job. Name one area and one level in each line.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Skills are practical abilities (typing fast, knowing menus); competence adds knowledge, judgement and attitudes (checking sources, protecting data). A fast typist who shares passwords has skills but not competence.
2. Information and data literacy; communication and collaboration; digital content creation; safety; problem solving.
3. (a) safety; (b) information and data literacy; (c) digital content creation; (d) problem solving.
4. Foundation (levels 1–2).
5. Software takes over routine tasks, so workers must use, check and combine digital tools; and tools change, so workers must keep learning.
6. For example, producer: plans in the cloud (2), budgets in spreadsheets (1).
7. Your own answer. Each line names an area and a level, for example "Safety — intermediate: I use a screen lock and a code on my phone for all accounts."
:::
